headline: Canarsie Pier at Dawn: Fluke to Five Pounds While the Ocean Stays Angry
subhead: With the surf blown out at Breezy and Rockaway, the smart money moved into the bay's channels — and got rewarded.
body_markdown:
I launched the kayak off Canarsie Pier at 5:40 Tuesday morning because the ocean gave me no other choice. Buoy readings off the Bight have been sitting around 71 to 72 degrees with three-foot swell on a short four-second period — that's not surf you fish comfortably from a beach chair, and it's definitely not surf you paddle into. So I did what I've done for twenty years when the Atlantic gets sloppy: I turned my back on it and went to work the flats and channels between Ruffle Bar and Grassy Bay, where the water lies down even when the wind won't.

Good call. I had four fluke in the yak before seven, biggest going about five pounds, all on a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the drop from eight feet down to sixteen off the edge of the flat. The current there was still building on the incoming, and fluke were sitting right on that seam where the mud gives way to sand. If you're working this spot from a boat, same drill — short drifts, bucktail bouncing bottom, and don't be afraid to let it sit dead still for a second before the next hop. That's usually when they eat.

The bay itself has been carrying more bait than I've seen in a few Julys — peanut bunker pushing through Beach Channel, small mullet stacked along the marsh edges by North Channel Bridge. That bait is exactly why the fluke bite has stayed dependable even with the ocean acting up. When the front is rough, forage gets squeezed into the estuary, and predators follow the food, not the tide charts. I talked to a guy at the Motts Basin ramp Wednesday who'd boxed a limit of keeper fluke in that same stretch, plus two shorts he tossed back — a good, honest morning, not a giveaway, but a real bite if you put in the drift time.

Stripers are trickier right now, and I'll be straight with you — the daytime bay bite has gone quiet the way it always does in mid-July heat. Bass don't love warm, thin water in bright sun, and Jamaica Bay's shallow flats heat up fast under a July sun. What's working is night fishing at Marine Parkway Bridge, and it's working the way it always has for me: get there an hour before the tide turns to outgoing, park tight to the pilings on the Rockaway side, and swim a white bucktail or a fresh eel through the shadow lines the lights throw on the water. I had two fish over 28 inches Thursday night doing exactly that, both within the first hour of the ebb, both right where the current started ripping off the structure. After that first hour of hard water movement, the bite shuts down fast — so don't sleep in and expect it to still be happening at midnight.

Bluefish have been the most reliable thing in the whole system. Rockaway Inlet has had blitzy pockets on the last of the outgoing, birds working tight over bunker pods, choppers in the 3 to 5 pound range slashing metal — I've been throwing a 1-ounce Deadly Dick and hooking up on almost every other cast when I find the right push of water off the Breezy Point side. If you're fishing from the rocks at Breezy, that outgoing water funneling past the point is your window; go an hour either side of the tide change and you'll likely find something busting on top, even with the ocean beyond the inlet still churned up and unfishable.

Porgies are around Cross Bay Bridge in decent numbers, nothing spectacular but steady — bloodworms or a chunk of clam on a high-low rig, fished tight to the pilings on the bottom half of the tide, will get you a nice mess for the pan. I haven't heard a single solid weakfish report out of the bay this year, which tracks with what's been happening system-wide — that fishery just isn't what it used to be here, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you want tiderunners, you're better off putting your time into bass and fluke right now and treating any weakfish as a bonus, not a target.

Looking at the week ahead, the ocean isn't likely to settle fast — that swell period and the wind pattern feeding it suggest Breezy and Rockaway Beach stay lumpy through at least the weekend. That's fine by me. It means another week of leaning on the bay's structure and current edges instead of fighting whitewater. If I had one trip to make, I'd launch out of Canarsie or Motts Basin on the front half of an outgoing tide, work the Ruffle Bar flats for fluke while the water's still moving, then slide over to Marine Parkway right at dusk to catch that first hour of ebb for bass. Two access points, one tide cycle, and you've covered both bites without burning a full tank of gas. Keep an eye on the bunker schools moving through the inlet too — wherever they stack up tight, the blues and the bigger bass won't be far behind.
